body:
What does efficiency mean in hydrogen production?

Producing hydrogen requires an input of energy. Electrolyser efficiency compares the chemical energy stored in the hydrogen with the electricity used to produce it, using a stated method of measurement.

Hydrogen has a lower heating value (LHV) of approximately 33.3 kWh per kg. LHV is one way of measuring a fuel's usable chemical energy, excluding the heat that could be recovered by condensing the water vapour produced during its use.

Consider a purely illustrative case in which an electrolyser uses 50 kWh of electricity to produce 1 kg of hydrogen. On an LHV basis:

Efficiency = (33.3 ÷ 50) × 100 = approximately 66.6%

This is an explanation of the calculation, not a claim that every electrolyser operates at 66.6% efficiency. Actual efficiency varies with the technology, operating conditions and whether auxiliary equipment is included.

Where does energy get used?

Green hydrogen passes through several energy-consuming stages:

  • Production: electricity is consumed during electrolysis, and some energy becomes heat rather than stored hydrogen energy.
  • Preparation: purification, drying and compression may require further energy.
  • Storage and transport: compression, liquefaction, cooling and movement can add energy requirements.
  • Final use: converting hydrogen back into electricity in a fuel cell involves another conversion loss.

Consequently, the electricity recovered after producing, storing and reconverting hydrogen is less than the electricity originally supplied. This is why hydrogen is best considered for applications that benefit from its chemical properties or storage characteristics, rather than for every task that electricity could perform directly.

Water use and local environmental considerations

The theoretical chemical requirement is about 9 litres of water per kg of hydrogen. Real facilities may need additional water for treatment or cooling, depending on the process and water-recovery arrangements.

In a water-scarce region, water availability becomes an important location factor. Desalinated seawater may be considered in coastal locations, but desalination and purification require additional infrastructure and energy. Using renewable electricity does not remove the need to assess water supply and other local environmental effects.

What determines the cost?

Green hydrogen must compete with hydrogen made from fossil fuels, often at established industrial sites. The main influences on production and delivered cost include:

  • Electricity price: electrolysis consumes substantial electricity, so affordable renewable power is important.
  • Electrolyser cost and use: equipment is expensive, and a plant producing hydrogen for relatively few hours must spread its fixed costs over fewer kilograms.
  • Renewable-power availability: cheap electricity is useful, but strongly variable supply can affect how often an electrolyser operates.
  • Water supply and treatment: purified water must be available at acceptable cost and with suitable environmental safeguards.
  • Storage and delivery: compression, liquefaction, transport and associated infrastructure increase the delivered cost.
  • Scale and demand: nearby industrial customers and shared infrastructure can reduce some logistical difficulties.

Why is green hydrogen not used everywhere?

Where electricity can be used directly, such as in many ordinary electrical appliances and battery-electric vehicles, direct use often avoids conversion steps and can be more energy-efficient.

Hydrogen becomes more attractive where its role is difficult to replace with direct electricity: manufacturing ammonia, supplying suitable refining processes, acting as a reducing agent in certain ironmaking routes, or meeting selected long-duration storage and heavy-transport requirements.

Cost competitiveness should not be assumed merely because a country has abundant solar or wind resources. Production, water supply, equipment utilisation, storage infrastructure and dependable demand all matter.

Global context

According to the International Energy Agency's Global Hydrogen Review 2026, global hydrogen demand exceeded 100 million tonnes in 2025. Almost all demand was associated with traditional industrial and refining uses. Low-emissions hydrogen production reached nearly 1 million tonnes in 2025, remaining less than 1% of total hydrogen production.

These are 2025 global data reported in 2026, not Indian production figures or targets. They show that the potential applications of low-emission hydrogen are much larger than its actual deployment at that time.

Prelims focus

  • Hydrogen's lower heating value is approximately 33.3 kWh per kg.
  • Electrolysis requires an electrical-energy input; efficiency depends on the defined measurement boundary.
  • Compression, liquefaction and conversion back to electricity add energy requirements or losses.
  • Electricity price and electrolyser utilisation strongly affect green-hydrogen cost.
  • Direct electrification is often more energy-efficient where it can perform the same task.
  • Trap: High energy content per kilogram does not mean that hydrogen is cheap to store, transport or convert back into electricity.

[Sources: U.S. Department of Energy, DOE Technical Targets for Onboard Hydrogen Storage for Light-Duty Vehicles, Useful Constants, lower heating value of hydrogen; U.S. Department of Energy, Technical Targets for Liquid Alkaline Electrolysis, table Technical Targets for Liquid Alkaline Electrolyzer Stacks and Systems (updated 29 May 2026); U.S. Department of Energy, Liquid Hydrogen Delivery, section Liquefaction (updated 8 June 2026); Press Information Bureau, Green Hydrogen: Emerging Pillar of India's Clean Energy Transition, section How Is Green Hydrogen Produced?, 28 October 2026; International Energy Agency, Global Hydrogen Review 2026, Executive Summary, sections Low-emissions hydrogen progressed in 2025 and Hydrogen-based fuels can help to diversify the energy sector, June 2026.]

title: Efficiency, Water Requirements and the Economics of Green Hydrogen

body:
Why does India support green hydrogen?

India has substantial solar and wind resources and major industries that use hydrogen. Green-hydrogen production offers an opportunity to replace part of the fossil-derived hydrogen used in fertiliser plants, petroleum refineries and other industries.

Domestic production may also reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels and create opportunities for the supply of low-emission industrial products. However, commercial success depends on affordable renewable power, water availability, production technology, storage facilities and customers willing to use the hydrogen.

National Green Hydrogen Mission

The Union Cabinet approved the National Green Hydrogen Mission (NGHM) in January 2023. The Mission is implemented by the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE).

Its approved financial outlay is ₹19,744 crore. Its major production objective is to establish capacity for at least 5 million metric tonnes of green hydrogen per year by 2030.

The Mission supports production, domestic electrolyser manufacturing, research, demonstration projects, standards and related infrastructure. The Strategic Interventions for Green Hydrogen Transition (SIGHT) programme supports green-hydrogen production and domestic electrolyser manufacturing through incentives. Its allocation is ₹17,490 crore up to 2029–30.

A 2030 target is not an achieved production figure. A project receiving incentives or an award is also not necessarily a commissioned or operating plant. These stages must be distinguished when interpreting government data.

Production capacity: targets, awards and commissioned projects

The following figures were reported in the Press Information Bureau backgrounder published on 28 October 2026. They have different meanings and, where stated, different reference periods.

IndicatorReported figure and status
National production objectiveAt least 5 million metric tonnes of annual capacity by 2030; target
Commissioned green-hydrogen capacityAbout 8,000 tonnes per year by February 2026; commissioned
Production capacity awarded incentives8,62,000 tonnes per year; incentive awards, not proof of commissioning
Electrolyser manufacturing capacity awarded incentives3,000 MW per year across 15 companies; manufacturing incentive awards

These figures show that the Mission's 2030 ambition is much larger than the capacity reported as commissioned by February 2026. They should not be added together as if each represented operational hydrogen production.

Why is Gujarat important?

Gujarat has several characteristics relevant to green-hydrogen development:

  • Solar resources: western Gujarat, including Kachchh, offers locations with strong solar-energy potential.
  • Wind resources: Kachchh and parts of coastal Gujarat have favourable conditions for wind-energy development.
  • Industrial demand: Gujarat has major petroleum, chemical and fertiliser-related industries where hydrogen or hydrogen-derived chemicals are relevant.
  • Ports and coastal location: suitable ports can support equipment movement and potential trade in hydrogen-derived products, particularly ammonia.
  • Water considerations: access to water, its treatment and sustainable supply must be assessed, especially in dry regions.

The presence of good solar and wind resources creates an opportunity, but it does not establish that every proposed hydrogen facility is economically viable or operational.

Kandla and India's recognised green-hydrogen hubs

By the information published on 28 October 2026, MNRE had recognised the following ports as green-hydrogen hubs:

  • Deendayal Port, Kandla in Gujarat.
  • V. O. Chidambaranar Port, Tuticorin in Tamil Nadu.
  • Paradip Port in Odisha.

A 1 MW green-hydrogen plant at Kandla Port was commissioned in July 2025. Commissioned means that the facility had reached an operational commissioning stage; it should not be confused with larger projects that are merely announced or planned.

The 28 October 2026 government backgrounder also listed Gujarat among the states with a notified dedicated green-hydrogen policy.

How a green-hydrogen hub can work

A hydrogen hub brings producers, users and supporting facilities into a connected industrial area. For example, renewable electricity can supply an electrolyser near a port or industrial cluster. The hydrogen can serve nearby industry, be converted into ammonia or be prepared for onward transport.

Producing hydrogen close to large users reduces the distance over which a difficult-to-transport gas must travel. Shared facilities and dependable customers may improve practical viability, although costs, infrastructure and environmental conditions still have to be evaluated.

Green hydrogen at a glance

For objective examinations, the most important distinction is between hydrogen's chemistry, the process used to produce it, its method of storage and its final application. All 4 determine whether a statement about green hydrogen is correct.

Prelims focus

  • The National Green Hydrogen Mission was approved in January 2023 and is implemented by MNRE.
  • The Mission's approved outlay is ₹19,744 crore.
  • Its 2030 objective is at least 5 million metric tonnes of annual green-hydrogen production capacity.
  • SIGHT supports green-hydrogen production and domestic electrolyser manufacturing.
  • Deendayal Port at Kandla, Gujarat, is one of India's recognised green-hydrogen hubs.
  • A 1 MW green-hydrogen plant was commissioned at Kandla Port in July 2025.
  • Trap: Capacity awarded incentives is not the same as commissioned production capacity.

[Sources: NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12 Geography, Chapter 7, Mineral and Energy Resources, pp. 81–83, sections Non-Conventional Energy Sources, Solar Energy and Wind Energy; Press Information Bureau, Green Hydrogen: Emerging Pillar of India's Clean Energy Transition, sections NGHM: A Mission for the Whole Ecosystem, SIGHT, Key Progress, Green Hydrogen Hubs and Hydrogen Valley Innovation Clusters and State-level Initiatives, published 28 October 2026. Status figures refer to the periods specified in that publication and are presented at the content cutoff of 16 November 2026.]
